newsitem.title: USA: HSBC, Dean Witter tops in February payrolls poll.
newsitem.headline: HSBC, Dean Witter tops in February payrolls poll.

text.p: Economists at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc and HSBC Securities Inc came closest to projecting the amount of U.S. payrolls growth for February in a recent Reuters poll.
The two firms had forecast a gain of 325,000, just below the actual figure of 339,000.
On average, analysts surveyed last Friday had projected payrolls grew by 230,000 last month, compared to a revised January reading of 247,000 reported this Friday.
Mild weather and solid retail sales performance figured into the above-consensus forecast of William Sullivan, senior vice president and director of fixed-income research at Dean Witter.

"We felt that you had to acknowledge the unusually mild winter," Sullivan said. "Reports we had gleaned from around the country suggested that construction activity was unusually strong in February in a lot of cold-weather areas."
Perhaps a more long-term trend is the apparent willingness of retail-sector employees to hire more workers, Sullivan said.

"The consumer has picked up interest in spending, (and) there's pressure on the retail trade to start hiring more aggressively," he said. "There's a new environment for retail, where businesses are willing to take on more workers."
Besides the gains in construction and retail employment, government-sector hiring helped boost payrolls last month, Sullivan said.
Jonathan Basile, an economist at HSBC Securities, said many analysts had been expecting seasonal factors to subtract from the payrolls gains.
"We didn't think the seasonals quirk was going to occur," Basile said. "Some analysts had been expecting that to take out something like 100,000 from the payrolls number."
Another clue came from jobless claims, the economist said.
"The four-week moving average of jobless claims in the survey weeks between January and February (employment reports) dropped 9.0 percent," he said.
In the past three years, similar declines in claims resulted, on average, in monthly payrolls increases of 350,000, Basile said.
Looking ahead, neither Sullivan nor Basile had prepared a forecast for March jobs growth, although Basile said he would hazard a guess.
